summary: Pupils aged 12–13 learn that reacting an acid does not make matter vanish — atoms are rearranged into NEW substances: a salt plus water when the acid is neutralised by an alkali or a metal oxide/hydroxide, or a salt plus hydrogen when a reactive metal reacts. Learners anchor the reaction families (acid + metal → salt + hydrogen, shown with reactive metals such as magnesium, zinc or iron and dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid; acid + alkali → salt + water; acid + metal oxide or metal hydroxide → salt + water), apply a predictable salt-naming rule (the acid fixes the ending: hydrochloric→chloride, sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate; the metal or metal-in-the-base gives the first word), observe family-distinguishing signatures (hydrogen squeaky-pop test; indicator reaching pH 7), and recover the dissolved salt by evaporation to crystals. Work stays at word-equation level; symbol equations, state symbols and moles are deferred. Activities are proposals; concrete bench chemistry and manipulable models are complementary ways to run the predict–observe–name loop.
misconceptions: Thinking neutralisation makes the acid 'disappear' rather than converting it into a salt plus water.
Believing a salt means only table salt (sodium chloride), not a whole family of compounds.
Assuming every acid reaction gives off a gas — confusing acid + metal (hydrogen released) with acid + alkali (no gas, water formed).
Mixing up the salt endings, e.g. expecting sulfuric acid to give a 'sulfide' rather than a sulfate.
Thinking the dissolved salt is 'gone' once it is in solution, rather than recoverable by evaporation.

activities.title: The salt maker: run reactions, name the salt, write the word equation
steps: Choose dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid and pair it with a moderately reactive metal such as magnesium, zinc or iron (not copper, which does not react, and never sodium or potassium); observe bubbles rising and test the gas at the mouth of the tube with a lit splint — a squeaky pop signals hydrogen. (Nitric acid is fine for the naming rule with alkalis and oxides, but with metals it usually gives nitrogen oxides rather than hydrogen, so it is not used for this run.)

Keep the same acid but this time use an alkali (e.g. sodium hydroxide solution) instead of the metal; with indicator already in the acid, add the alkali gradually, a little at a time — observe that there is no fizz, and watch the indicator change until it shows pH 7 (neutralisation), giving salt + water.

After each run, state the salt's full name before it is written out, deriving the surname from the acid (chloride/sulfate/nitrate) and the first word from the metal or the metal in the alkali, then write the complete word equation (e.g. magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen).

Finish by evaporating the neutral solution to drive off the water and leave visible salt crystals in the dish (for purer crystals, repeat the neutralisation with the same volumes but no indicator, because indicator left in the solution colours the salt).

Repeat with new pairings — acid/reactive metal (dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid), acid/alkali, and acid/metal oxide or hydroxide (e.g. copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water) — so the naming rule generalises across examples rather than being memorised as a list.
activities.insight: Neutralising or reacting an acid converts it into a real, recoverable salt (plus hydrogen or water) — matter is conserved and rearranged, not destroyed — and the salt's name follows predictably from the acid and the metal.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: what is left when the water evaporates?
steps: Neutralise an acid with an alkali until the indicator reads pH 7.
BEFORE evaporating, write down a prediction: if all the water is driven off, what (if anything) will remain, and WHY?
Evaporate the water and compare the result with the prediction.
Write the word equation for what happened (acid + alkali → salt + water) and explain in words why 'neutral' does not mean 'empty'.
activities.insight: A 'cancelled to nothing' model predicts an empty dish; the solid salt crystals that remain disprove it. Neutralisation produces a salt plus water, and mass is conserved as atoms rearrange into new products.

activities.title: Complete and name: word-equation practice across families
steps: Complete partial word equations, e.g. 'sulfuric acid + zinc → zinc ____ + ____', filling both the salt surname and the gas.
Match each acid to its salt ending: hydrochloric→chloride, sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate.
Decide, for a given pairing, whether hydrogen or water is produced, and justify the choice by naming the family (acid+reactive metal vs acid+alkali or acid+metal oxide/hydroxide).
Name the salt from an unfamiliar acid/base pair (e.g. hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide → potassium chloride + water) and state why it is not sodium chloride.
State the pH at the neutralisation endpoint (7) and name the gas test for hydrogen (lit splint, squeaky pop).
activities.insight: The productive salt-naming rule and the family distinction (hydrogen vs water) can be applied to new pairings, not just recognised in familiar ones.

activities.title: Vocabulary and family contrast (introductory scaffold)
steps: Study a labelled picture of a neutralisation (acid + alkali → salt + water), revealing the names of the acid, the alkali, the salt crystals and the role of each part.
Contrast a side-by-side pair of the two reaction families and say, for each, whether a gas is released and what the other product is.
Connect the vocabulary to a real application: indigestion tablets neutralise stomach acid, and treating acidic soil raises its pH.
activities.insight: Names and family vocabulary (acid, alkali, salt, neutralisation, hydrogen) and the two product patterns are introduced before learners run and generalise them.

checkQuestion: I mix hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide (an alkali) in the right amounts and the mixture ends up neutral, pH 7. A student says 'so now there's nothing left — they cancelled each other out to nothing.' Is that right — what is actually in the beaker now? Then explain what neutralisation really produces.
checkAnswer: No — nothing vanished. Neutralisation produces a SALT plus WATER: here sodium chloride dissolved in water (acid + alkali → salt + water). 'Neutral' means the acidity and alkalinity are balanced, not that matter disappeared — the atoms rearranged into new products (mass is conserved). Full marks name salt + water as the products and reject 'cancelled to nothing'.
